worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

 

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $36{x}^{2}=(6x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{36{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{(6x)^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡6x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
